questions.explanation: For the center of mass to be at the origin, the net moment about the origin must be zero: m⋅a+M⋅(−3a)m+M=0    ⟹    m a−3a M=0    ⟹    m=3 M    ⟹    M=m3.m a + M (-3a)/m + M = 0 \;\;\;\; m\,a - 3a\,M = 0 \;\;\;\; m = 3\,M \;\;\;\; M = m/3.

questions.question: A cricket bat is cut at the location of its centre of mass as shown. Then
options: The two pieces will have the same mass
The bottom piece will have larger mass
The handle piece will have larger mass
Mass of handle piece is double the mass of bottom piece
questions.explanation: Because a cricket bat is thicker/heavier at its blade end, the center of mass lies closer to that heavier (lower) portion. Cutting the bat at its center of mass thus leaves a shorter (blade) piece and a longer (handle) piece. Nonetheless, because the lower portion is denser (more mass per unit length), the bottom piece has the larger mass.

questions.question: Consider following statements [1] {CM} of a uniform semicircular disc of radius {R}=2 {R} / π from the centre [2] {CM} of a uniform semicircular ring of radius {R}=4 {R} / 3 π from the centre [3] {CM} of a solid hemisphere of radius {R}=4 {R} / 3 π from the centre [4] {CM} of a hemisphere shell of radius R=R / 2 from the centre Which statements are correct?
questions.explanation: Using the standard results (as found in NCERT or derived via integration): Semicircular disk (2D) has its CM at 4R3π{4R}{3π} from the center, not 2Rπ.{2R}{π}. Semicircular ring (1D) has its CM at 2Rπ{2R}{π} from the center, not 4R3π.{4R}{3π}. Solid hemisphere (3D) has its CM at 3R8{3R}{8} from the flat face, which does not equal 4R3π.{4R}{3π}. Hemispherical shell (thin “bowl”) has its CM at R2{R}{2} from the flat face (the usual “center” in such problems). Hence only statement (4) is correct.

questions.question: In a one-dimensional perfectly elastic collision, the relative velocity of approach before collision is equal to
options: equal to sum of the velocities of the bodies
less than the relative velocity of separation after collision
greater than the relative velocity of separation after collision
equal to relative velocity of separation after collision
questions.explanation: In a one-dimensional elastic collision, the relative velocity of approach before collision is equal to relative velocity of separation after collision (coefficient of restitution, e = 1)

questions.question: In elastic collision, I. initial kinetic energy is equal to the final kinetic energy. II. kinetic energy during the collision time t is constant. III. total momentum is conserved. Which of the above statements is/are correct?
questions.explanation: (i) Statement I is correct: in an elastic collision, total initial kinetic energy equals total final kinetic energy.(ii) Statement II is incorrect: during the short collision interval, the kinetic energy can be temporarily shared as internal potential energy (deformation, etc.). Only at the start and end of the collision does the total kinetic energy equal its initial/final value.(iii) Statement III is correct: total linear momentum is conserved in all collisions (elastic or inelastic). Hence the correct statements are I and III, matching Option B.

questions.question: The bob (mass m ) of a simple pendulum of length {L} is held horizontal and then released. It collides elastically with a block of equal mass lying on a frictionless table. The kinetic energy of the block will be
questions.explanation: Right before colliding with the block, the bob (mass mm) has converted all of its initial potential energy (released from the horizontal) into kinetic energy. The change in height is LL, so its speed is v  =  2gL.v \;=\;√(2gL). Because the collision is elastic and both masses are equal (mm), the standard one‐dimensional result is that the incoming mass comes to rest and the originally stationary mass takes on the entire velocity vv. Hence, the block’s kinetic energy is K  =  12 m v²  =  12 m (2gL)  =  m g L.K \;=\;12\,m\,v² \;=\;12\,m\,(2gL) \;=\;m\,g\,L. Answer: m g Lm\,g\,L.
